prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: The depth map shows a top-down kitchen counter layout about 0.5–0.7 metres below and in front of the camera wearer, with the wearer's lower torso at the bottom edge (0.2–0.3 metres) and two arms extending forward within arm's reach (0.3–0.6 metres). Across frames 1 to 4, the wearer's right hand moves from the centre chopping board to the right bag of greens while the left hand reaches toward the potatoes, then lifts upward toward the knife block on the left (brightening to ~0.3 metres in frame 3) and drops down to a carton at the lower left in frame 4. In frame 5, the camera turns right to face a stove top (0.6–0.9 metres away) while the right hand holds a knife blade at ~0.4 metres, and a second person stands to the far right (0.8–1.5 metres away, ~0.7 metres right of the wearer) facing the counter and away from the camera wearer with their head and upper torso out of view. This map makes the 3D relief of the food bags, knife handles, and the vertical height of the raised left hand in frame 3 and upright knife blade in frame 5 much clearer than in the RGB image. However, the monocular depth estimation is unreliable along the top edge—where the upright recipe card, spice rack, and upper wall (actually ~0.6–0.8 metres away) appear overly bright as if closer than the counter—and on the glossy black stove top, which appears artificially dark and deep.
descriptions.segmentation: The segmentation map isolates discrete foreground regions on the counter within 0.3–0.7 metres of the camera wearer, primarily tracking the wearer's left and right forearms as separate 'person' instances spaced ~0.2–0.4 metres apart at the bottom of frames 1–5. In frames 1, 2, and 5, it also detects the partially visible second person at the far bottom-right and right edge (~0.8–1.5 metres away, facing the counter to the right and not looking at the wearer) as separate 'person' masks for their lower legs/feet and right hand reaching onto the counter within their own arm's reach. While the map helps separate overlapping object boundaries—such as distinguishing the knife handles ('scissors') from the wooden block in frame 3, the bag of greens ('broccoli') from the right hand in frame 4, and the second person's limbs from the floor and counter in frame 5—it misses most scene elements including the chopping board, lettuce, potatoes, stove, and recipe card. The map is highly unreliable in its class labels and temporal consistency, misclassifying spice jars as 'donut' or 'bottle', knife handles as 'scissors', the wearer's left hand as 'cell phone' in frame 1, and greens as 'broccoli', while completely dropping the wearer's left arm in frame 4 and the held knife in frame 5.
descriptions.pose: The pose map tracks the 2D skeletal keypoints of the camera wearer's hands (in magenta) within 0.3–0.6 metres in front of and below the camera across frames 1–4, and the lower-body skeleton (in yellow) of the second person on the far right (~1.0–1.5 metres away) in frame 5. In frames 1 and 2, both of the wearer's hands are detected with fingers splayed above the counter (~0.2–0.3 metres apart), shifting rightward from the potatoes and board in frame 1 to the potatoes and greens bag in frame 2; in frames 3 and 4, only the right hand remains detected on the greens bag while the wearer turns right in frame 5. The yellow body keypoints in frame 5 trace the second person's hips, knees, and ankles standing on the floor to the right of the stove, showing their lower body oriented toward the counter and away from the camera wearer while their upper body is occluded by the frame boundary. These skeletons make exact finger articulation and joint angles on the cluttered counter and dark trousers much easier to see than in the RGB strip alone. However, the pose map is unreliable whenever limbs are blurred, foreshortened, or holding objects, failing to detect the wearer's raised left hand in frame 3, the left hand at the bottom-left edge in frame 4, the knife-gripping right hand in frame 5, and the second person's visible foot in frame 1 and hand in frame 5.
